home.statementHtml: Most calculators make you translate your maths into their notation. This one does not.

statementNotes.dd: A one-line display forces you to flatten a fraction, an integral or a surd into a string of brackets — and that translation is where the marks get lost.
The natural textbook display renders the expression the way it is printed in the book, so what you type is what you meant, and you can see it before you press equals.
Fewer input errors, faster checking, and a calculator that carries from algebra through to an engineering degree.

home.pillarsLede: Not a range. One instrument, chosen because it covers the whole span from a first trigonometry class to a final-year engineering paper without ever being the limiting factor.

pillars.title: Reads like the textbook
pillars.body: Fractions stacked, roots under the radical, integrals with proper limits. You check your input by looking at it, not by counting brackets.

pillars.title: 552 functions, one menu
pillars.body: Statistics, matrices, vectors, complex numbers, base-n, equation solving and a spreadsheet — all reachable from a single MENU key rather than three layers of SHIFT.

pillars.title: Solar first, battery second
pillars.body: It runs off the light in the room and only draws on the cell when the light goes. No dead calculator on the morning of an exam.

detail.title: What it is, and what it actually does
detail.lede: The FX-991EX is a non-programmable scientific calculator built around one idea: the calculator should display mathematics the way it is written, not the way a 1980s seven-segment display forced it to be written. Everything else follows from that.

blocks.heading: The display shows the maths, not a transcription of it
blocks.body: A four-line dot-matrix display renders expressions in their printed form — a fraction as a fraction, a root under its radical, an integral with its limits in place. It matters more than it sounds. On a single-line calculator you flatten the expression into brackets before you type it, and that flattening is where mistakes are made and never spotted. Here you read back what you entered and compare it against the page.
blocks.imageAlt: Close crop of the four-line dot-matrix display showing the function menu

blocks.heading: 552 functions, reachable without a manual
blocks.body: Statistics and regression, matrices to 4 × 4, vectors, complex numbers, base-n arithmetic, numerical integration and differentiation, an equation solver, a table generator and a spreadsheet mode. All of it sits behind one MENU key instead of a second and third shift layer, which is the difference between a feature existing and a feature being used.
blocks.imageAlt: Close crop of the numeric keypad with the blue DEL and AC keys

blocks.heading: Sized for a hand and an exam desk
blocks.body: Slim enough to sit beside a paper without crowding it, with a slide-on hard cover that protects the keypad in a bag and doubles as a stand. Non-programmable by design, which is precisely what makes it admissible in the exam rooms that ban everything else.
blocks.imageAlt: The calculator held in one hand, showing its scale

scenarios.title: Algebra, trigonometry, and a syllabus that keeps growing
scenarios.body: The point at which most students buy their first scientific calculator, and the point at which most buy the wrong one. Anything that cannot display a stacked fraction will be replaced within two years.
steps: Read it back against the page

scenarios.title: Engineering, calculus and linear algebra coursework
scenarios.body: Matrices, vectors, complex numbers and numerical integration in one device, so problem sheets do not require a laptop. The functions that matter at degree level are the ones buried two menus deep on cheaper models.
steps: Read the result in full precision

scenarios.title: Data sets, regression and distributions
scenarios.body: Spreadsheet mode takes a column of data directly, so you are not re-keying a data set every time you want a different statistic. Regression and distribution functions read from the same table.

scenarios.title: The one on the permitted list
scenarios.body: Non-programmable, no wireless, no stored text. That is the specification exam boards actually check, and it is why a calculator like this is admissible where a graphing model is confiscated at the door.

scenarios.title: Unit conversion, constants and quick checks
scenarios.body: Built-in scientific constants and unit conversions cover the routine arithmetic of a lab notebook without a lookup table. Light enough to live in a bag permanently.

faq.a: It is non-programmable, which is the property most boards test for. Always check the specific list published by your own exam board — that list is the authority, not us.
It runs on solar in normal room light and falls back to an LR44 cell when the light is poor. The cell is fitted and typically lasts around two years.
No. It generates tables of values rather than plotting curves. If you need plotting you want a graphing calculator — and you should check whether your exam board permits one.

faq.q: What is the difference from a cheaper scientific calculator?
faq.a: The display and the function count. A basic model shows one line and around 240 functions; this shows four lines in textbook notation and covers 552, including matrices, vectors and the spreadsheet.
